item.title: Functional Network Organization Underlying Individual Differences in False Feedback Susceptibility: A Graph Theoretical Analysis
item.author: J. Patchitt, T. Karapanagiotidis, S. N. Garfinkel, M. Miller, M. Tsakiris, A. Clark, H. D. Critchley
item.content:encoded: Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false feedback (sFFB) predict altered network topography between regions previously implicated in sFFB. This work supports an interoceptive integration model of sFFB and highlights the importance of network topology in determining how individuals weigh and integrate internal and external physiological information during emotional processing.Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false physiological feedback reflect variations in interoceptive processing, yet the underlying neural network mechanisms remain unclear. We analyzed resting-state functional connectivity using graph theoretical approaches in 41 healthy adults who completed a somatosensory false feedback paradigm. Nine regions of interest were defined from previous activation analyses, and network topology metrics including local efficiency, clustering coefficient, centrality measures, and path length were calculated across multiple thresholds. Three distinct patterns of network organization predicted false feedback susceptibility. Individuals more susceptible to false feedback showed: (1) increased posterior insula eccentricity, indicating network peripheralization of this key interoceptive region; (2) consistent orbitofrontal cortex segregation across multiple metrics including increased path length and decreased centrality measures; and (3) cerebellar network reconfiguration with reduced local efficiency but increased betweenness centrality. Somatosensory false feedback susceptibility reflects specific alterations in functional network topology, particularly reduced integration of interoceptive regions (posterior insula) and emotional appraisal systems (orbitofrontal cortex). These findings support a network-based model where interoceptive processing depends on efficient integration between visceral sensation, emotional evaluation, and cognitive control systems. Understanding these network properties may inform interventions targeting interoceptive awareness and emotional regulation.

item.title: Fitness level, but not sex, affects exercise-induced pain modulation
item.author: Zora Pia Gerbers
item.content:encoded: In a previous study by our group (Nold et al., 2025), we investigated exercise-induced pain modulation after high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise in a heterogeneous sample of diverse fitness levels. Exploratory analyses suggested an interaction of sex, fitness level, and drug treatment, indicating that males showed increasing hypoalgesia after high- compared to low-intensity exercise with increasing fitness levels, which was diminished when naloxone was administered. In contrast, these effects were not evident in females. These exploratory findings warranted further investigation to determine if and to what extent exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level and/or sex. In this current study, we investigated an all-female sample (N=21) of high fitness levels using a similar paradigm as in the previous study, comparing heat and pressure pain ratings after high-intensity and low-intensity exercise. Our data show an interaction of exercise intensity and stimulus intensity in heat pain, with greater pain relief following high-intensity exercise, especially at the highest stimulus intensity. Despite results for pressure pain not reaching significance, a similar trend was evident. These results suggest that females at a high fitness level also show exercise-induced pain modulation for high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise. Furthermore, we pooled the data of the current and previous study, providing evidence for fitness level but not sex to moderate exercise-induced pain modulation in heat pain. These findings suggest that exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level but not on sex.

item.title: Compensation of hyperexcitability with simulation-based inference
item.author: Tomoki Fukai
item.content:encoded: The activity of healthy neuronal networks is tightly regulated, and a shift toward hyperexcitability can cause various problems, such as epilepsies, memory deficits, and motor disorders. Numerous cellular, synaptic, and intrinsic mechanisms of hyperexcitability and compensatory mechanisms to restore healthy activity have been proposed. However, quantifying multiple compensatory mechanisms and their dependence on specific pathophysiological mechanisms has proven challenging, even in computational models. We use simulation-based inference to quantify the interactions of putative compensatory mechanisms in a spiking neuronal network model. Various parameters of the model can compensate for the changes in other parameters to maintain baseline activity, and we estimated their compensatory potential. Furthermore, specific causes of hyperexcitability – interneuron loss, excitatory recurrent synapses, and principal cell depolarization – have distinct compensatory mechanisms that can restore normal excitability. Our results show that spiking neuronal network simulators could generate hypotheses about the mechanisms of pathophysiological network mechanisms.

item.title: Glutamate receptor composition at Drosophila neuromuscular junctions depends on developmental stage and muscle identity
item.author: Yu Xiong
item.content:encoded: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of larval is widely used for studying synaptic transmission. Larval body wall muscles express five ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits that assemble into two tetrameric complexes, with subunit composition determining the strength and plasticity of synaptic transmission. Because NMJ function has been extensively characterized in larvae, it has commonly been assumed that adult fly NMJs share this molecular composition, despite substantial differences between life stages. Here, we systematically compare glutamate receptor expression across larval and adult muscles. We find that adult leg and flight muscles exhibit different iGluR expression than larvae, lacking expression of several receptors previously considered essential. Adjacent muscles within the adult femur express distinct iGluRs, suggesting specialization of flexor and extensor muscles. Finally, the glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluClα) is expressed extrasynaptically in adult but not larval muscle fibers. Our results reveal unexpected heterogeneity in glutamate receptor expression across muscles and developmental stages, demonstrating the need for muscle-specific analyses in flies and other animals.

item.title: Oxytocin neurons signal state-dependent transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal
item.author: Samantha Killmer
item.content:encoded: Core body temperature (Tb) is defended within narrow limits through thermoregulatory behaviors like huddling, nesting, and physical activity, as well as autonomic responses like brown fat thermogenesis. While Tb displays regulated fluctuations across different behavioral states and rest/arousal cycles, the neural control of these transitions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the relationship between oxytocin neurons of the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVN) and behavioral and autonomic thermoeffector pathways across physiological states in mice. First, we show that PVN neurons are activated during social thermoregulation. We then demonstrate that in vivo PVN calcium dynamics align with transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal. Counter to our initial hypothesis, these dynamics were observed in both social and non-social contexts. Using a computer vision model to track thermoeffector pathways, we demonstrate that precisely timed stimulation of PVN neurons during low-Tb resting states increases thermogenesis followed by behavioral arousal. We therefore suggest a model in which PVN neurons facilitate homeostatic state-dependent transitions in thermo-behavioral states.

item.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan
item.author: Zonglei Zhen
item.content:encoded: The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

item.title: Peripersonal space: a neural system mapping self–environment interaction ‘here and now’
item.author: Andrea Serino
item.content:encoded: The space surrounding the body where physical interactions with external stimuli occur is referred to as peripersonal space (PPS). Traditionally conceived as a spatial construct, PPS is better understood as a neural representation that integrates bodily inputs with external cues to predict body–object interactions. After summarizing its multisensory, motor, and plastic properties, this review draws on computational models to examine how PPS captures statistical regularities of body–object interactions. This predictive function may position PPS as an interface between self and environment, contributing to minimal self-consciousness and its alterations across states of consciousness and neuropsychiatric conditions. Recent findings extend this framework to the inner body, suggesting that interoceptive signals shape PPS and that PPS-related processing may influence immune responses.

item.title: Strength-based organizational approaches facilitate workplace opportunities for people from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds.
item.content:encoded: The workplace stands as one of the most powerful drivers of societal (in)equality. For employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds, it can represent both a ticket toward upward mobility and a consequential source of stigma. Four studies build on emerging strength-based research to test whether workplaces can challenge this stigma by creating overarching cultures that recognize the beneficial skills employees gain from their otherwise marginalized identities. Study 1 provided foundational insights into these “strength-based organizational approaches” and their implications for key outcomes derived from the State Authenticity as Fit to Environment model. Employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds were especially unlikely to report that their workplaces valued their identities and associated skills, which partially explained subsequent disparities in employees’ broad sense of comfort and efficacy at work. Studies 2a and 2b established these patterns experimentally by demonstrating that exposing participants to a workplace that does communicate a strength-based organizational approach facilitated these professionally productive outcomes while increasing participants’ likelihood of disclosing their marginalized identities within a job application task. Study 3 extended these findings to consider how the approaches may also indirectly expand employees’ equitable access to opportunity through reducing common biases among their supervisors. Randomly assigning workplace supervisors to briefly engage with a company that highlighted the value of employees’ lower socioeconomic status backgrounds increased supervisors’ positive evaluations and likelihood of promoting these employees by 38% relative to an active control condition. Collectively, these preregistered findings illuminate new opportunities to improve workplace functioning and pinpoint the organizational forces underlying person–context interactions. item.title: How we see relations: The case of containment and support.
item.content:encoded: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across, types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens (“in” or “on”) but rather as objects’ properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: Task-evoked pupillary responses reveal a role for attentional intensity in auditory discrimination.
item.content:encoded: Sensory discrimination has long been theorized to reflect a core cognitive function underlying intelligence. Building on this tradition, we examined whether task-evoked pupil responses, as an index of mental effort, relate to attention control (AC) and auditory discrimination ability. Using a large data set (N = 336), participants completed three adaptive auditory discrimination tasks (pitch, duration, loudness), a cognitive battery assessing AC, working memory capacity, and fluid intelligence, and pupillometry during task performance. Structural equation modeling confirmed that AC predicted auditory discrimination thresholds and fully mediated the relationship between task-evoked pupil dilation and performance. Trial-level multilevel models revealed that higher task difficulty and errors were associated with larger pupil dilations, especially in demanding tasks. Crucially, individuals with greater AC exhibited steeper increases in pupil dilation with rising task difficulty and were more resilient to performance declines. For high-AC individuals, large pupil responses predicted preserved accuracy; for low-AC individuals, they signaled compensatory effort with diminished success. These results suggest that AC governs both the extent and efficacy of mental effort, determining whether high arousal facilitates or fails to improve performance. This work refines classic resource models by demonstrating that cognitive effort, indexed via pupillometry, supports perception most effectively when guided by strong AC. Findings support a hierarchical model in which AC serves as the functional bridge between arousal, sensory discrimination, and higher order cognition. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: The orthographic mind: Orthographic imagery propensity correlates with semantic structure and sensory sensitivity.
item.content:encoded: Individuals differ in their habitual use of internal representational modes, including visual imagery, internal verbalization, and orthographic imagery (the mental simulation of written word forms). The present research examined whether such internal representational propensities relate to semantic organization and external information engagement. Across two studies (total N = 1,399), we assessed individuals’ internal representational modes using the Internal Representations Questionnaire and examined their associations with semantic structure (nine-word semantic rating experiments; N = 1,109) and external information engagement (sensory-processing sensitivity and mobile app usage). Orthographic imagery showed robust associations with both semantic geometry and external information engagement patterns: Individuals with stronger orthographic imagery showed greater cross-category semantic association strength, lower semantic conformity, and lower sensory-processing sensitivity. Internal verbalization was positively associated with within-category semantic cohesion, while visual imagery showed no reliable associations with semantic geometry and limited associations with real-world media engagement. Effects were modest but consistent across experiments. These findings suggest that internal representational modes function as stable weighting biases, subtly modulating semantic geometry and sensory-processing profiles. Such propensities therefore correspond to structured variations in cognition, rather than merely phenomenological differences in inner experience. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: Children can suppress salient distractors.
item.content:encoded: From a very young age, our perceptual system is particularly sensitive to salient events. When such events are irrelevant, adults can prevent them from capturing attention by suppressing the salient features and by prioritizing task-relevant information. Previous research suggests that both distractor-suppression and target-prioritization mechanisms are not yet fully developed at ages 5–6. However, this work has not clearly disentangled the two mechanisms. Here, we specifically investigated whether children can suppress the salient feature of an irrelevant distractor. Two groups of children (aged 5–6 and 8–9) searched for a shape-defined target among heterogeneously shaped nontargets. All items had the same color throughout the experiment, but on two thirds of the trials, one item (the singleton distractor) had a unique color that changed at the beginning of each block. We expected this distractor to interfere with search performance during the first half of each block (i.e., when its color was novel). The critical question was whether this interference would be reduced during the second block half (i.e., with enough experience with the distractor’s color). This finding would indicate that the children suppressed the salient distractor color. We found clear evidence for feature-based suppression, and this effect was similar for the two age groups. These findings indicate that feature-based suppression develops early and may already be established by ages 5–6. More broadly, they are consistent with accounts in which suppression emerges through implicit learning or habituation-like mechanisms that are operational early in development. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: Beliefs about the causal interdependence of virtues and vices.
item.content:encoded: How do people think different positive and negative moral traits (i.e., virtues and vices) affect one another? For example, do they think that improving one virtue (e.g., honesty) will facilitate improvements in another virtue (e.g., compassion)? Do people believe in “master virtues” that, when improved, have disproportionate positive impacts on other moral virtues? Here, we examine perceived causal interdependence among 15 moral virtues and 13 moral vices. Across four studies, participants indicated their beliefs about how increasing their virtues would impact their other virtues (Study 1; 275 Prolific participants), how increasing their vices would impact their other vices (Study 2; 423 undergraduate students), and how increases in virtues would affect vices (or vice versa; Studies 3 and 4; 337 undergraduate students and 298 Prolific participants). We find people generally believe in facilitation effects, where improving one trait improves other traits and worsening one trait worsens other traits. Specifically, people believe that increasing one virtue tends to increase other virtues (Study 1) and decrease other vices (Studies 3 and 4). Similarly, people believe that increasing one vice tends to increase other vices (Study 2) and decrease other virtues (Studies 3 and 4). Perceived trade-offs were rare and involved laziness and cowardice decreasing or being decreased by other vices. There was little evidence for beliefs in a “master virtue.” However, we find some evidence that people think cruelty and greed are disproportionately impactful “master vices.” These results enhance our understanding of lay moral concepts by painting a comprehensive picture of people’s beliefs about the causal interdependence among moral virtues and vices. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: Enacted love: Capitalization responses signal love, including toward strangers.
item.content:encoded: What behavior is seen as “love” and why does it matter? We theorize active-constructive responding to another’s disclosure of good news is prototypical “enacted love” and test hypotheses about implications for a loving person’s relationship development. We use three distinct methods—dyadic interactions between romantic couples (Study 1, N = 160), real spontaneous responses to a stranger’s good news (Study 2, N = 204), and observation of others’ real capitalization responses to a stranger’s good news (Studies 3–5, N = 97, 105, and 402, respectively)—to assess convergent and discriminant evidence for the construct. Study 2 uses experience sampling to track the development of capitalization respondents’ social lives over time. Studies 4 and 5 use within-subjects experiments to test hypotheses that loving behavior could influence others’ interactions with loving people. Results have theoretical implications for close relationships and the concept of “loving one’s neighbor,” plus practical implications for building bridges in a divided society. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: Investigating how reward retroactively improves memory for associations and items: A registered report.
item.content:encoded: Given we cannot remember all our experiences, it seems intuitive that we should prioritize events of consequence, like those that lead to a reward. However, rewards have had inconsistent effects on people’s memory for preceding neutral experiences in experiments, raising questions as to whether our minds are equipped to remember adaptively. Here, we used online testing in a registered report to investigate whether rewards tend to retroactively enhance certain types of memories. Consistent with prior research and theories involving how dopamine modulates the hippocampus, we hypothesized that reward would retroactively enhance memory in a delay-dependent manner, emerging only after a period of consolidation. Crucially, we further predicted that this long-delay modulation of memory would be stronger for associative memory than for item recognition—a factor not previously considered despite its clear theoretical grounding. Our planned confirmatory analyses did not reveal any evidence for retroactive effects of reward on either associative or item memory. However, in exploratory analyses examining only individuals who were behaviorally sensitive to the reward manipulation, as measured by an independent task, we found evidence that reward retroactively enhanced associative—but not item—memory in a delay-dependent manner. This work sheds light on important open questions about the mechanisms by which reward retroactively enhances memory, elucidating the conditions under which this key aspect of adaptive memory emerges. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: Whole-brain mapping of spinal-projecting neurons in larval zebrafish
item.author: Tom Welch
item.content:encoded: To elicit voluntary movements and integrative reflexes underlying behavior, the brain sends command signals to the spinal cord via specialized long-range descending neurons, known as spinal-projecting neurons (SPNs). The vast and widespread distribution of SPNs, combined with their complex long-distance connectivity, poses a significant challenge for mapping their anatomical organization and associating specific populations with distinct functions. Here, we took advantage of the transparency and genetic accessibility of larval zebrafish to uncover the fundamental principles of SPN anatomical organization in a teleost. Using an optical backfilling method relying on photoactivable GFP, we generate a whole-brain map of all neurons sending axons toward the spinal cord. This approach reveals far more SPNs than previously described through conventional strategies, offering an unparalleled opportunity to revisit distinct spinal-projecting nuclei distributed across the hindbrain, midbrain, and diencephalic structures. Combining information on cell location, morphology, and projection patterns, we propose tentative homological designations for zebrafish of SPN nuclei based on established descriptions in mammals and other vertebrates.

item.title: Revealing the benefit of eye motion for acuity under emulated cone loss
item.author: Ren Ng
item.content:encoded: Retinal degenerative diseases progressively erode the cone photoreceptor mosaic, reducing the retina’s spatial sampling power, yet visual acuity is remarkably resilient to cone loss. Prior work has shown that clinically normal visual acuity (20/25 or better) can persist despite up to 50% of cone cells being lost (Ratnam et al., 2013; Foote et al., 2018). However, studies on individuals with retinal degeneration cannot control for patients’ stage of disease progression, creating the need for an experimental paradigm that can mimic these diseases in healthy subjects. The Oz Vision system creates visual percepts through programmable, per-cell stimulation of thousands of cone cells. We reprogram this system to emulate cone loss in healthy eyes by withholding stimulation from a subset of randomly selected cones, rendering them inactive, in a method we term ‘cone dropout’. Using this approach, we characterize the visual system’s robustness to cone loss, showing that visual acuity declines nonlinearly with increasing cone dropout. Importantly, we uncover the compensatory benefit that eye motion provides under cone-deprived conditions, finding that at the highest level of dropout, a visual system with eye motion has an equivalent acuity to a static dropout condition with nearly twice as many sampling elements. Through analysis of eye motion and stimulation data, we find that this benefit arises from the additional information accumulated by ‘surviving’ cones as they sample more of the letter through fixational eye motion.

item.title: What can machine learning discover about the nature of emotion?
item.author: Kieran McVeigh, Andrew Smart, Ajay B. Satpute, Karen S. Quigley, Jordan E. Theriault-Brown, Lisa Feldman Barrett
item.content:encoded: The science of emotion increasingly relies on machine learning (ML) in the hope of making objective discoveries that resolve century-long debates. We examine research strategies in two main research traditions and show how confirmation bias can arise when theory-based hypotheses are evaluated using theory-laden sampling strategies, model specifications, and inferences. Each tradition manifests its theoretical differences in its ML methods, and, therefore, ML methods cannot settle those differences. The reciprocal relationships between starting assumptions, findings, and conclusions illustrate that ML investigations of emotion, like all scientific investigations, are never free from human experience and beliefs; however, they can be made less biased through a theory-aware research strategy to generate more justified knowledge about emotion.

item.title: Mate preferences and the compatibility puzzle
item.author: Paul W. Eastwick, Amy A.Z. Zhao, Brendan P. Zietsch
item.content:encoded: Researchers and laypeople commonly assume that romantic attraction depends, at least in part, on whether potential partners possess the traits that a person says they want. Yet recent studies suggest that such preference-matching effects (Preference × Trait statistical interactions) are often surprisingly small or even absent. Possible psychological explanations include (i) mate choice is multivariate, and so the matching effect for any given trait is heavily constrained, and (ii) traits permit flexible interpretations, in that the same trait can be interpreted differently depending on the partner to whom the trait belongs. Compatibility may derive not mainly from the matching of preferences and traits but rather from the way that two people recurrently extend and build upon shared positive experiences over time.

item.title: Serotonin signaling enhances phagocytosis by brain macrophages through Htr2b and alleviates brain injury after stroke
item.author: Peiying Li
item.content:encoded: The serotonin receptor Htr2b activation enhances lysosome biogenesis and phagocytic clearance of debris to mitigate neuroinflammation and brain injury after stroke. The study proposes a potential monocyte-derived macrophage-targeted immune therapy to improve neurological outcomes after ischemic stroke.

item.title: Ultrasound neuromodulation hypotheses on the directionality of effects and community resource
item.author: Timothy D Griffiths
item.content:encoded: Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) is a promising non-invasive technique for brain stimulation and focal neuromodulation. Research with humans and animal models has raised the possibility that TUS can be biased towards enhancing or suppressing neural function. Here, we first collate a set of hypotheses on the directionality of TUS effects and conduct an initial meta-analysis on available healthy human participant TUS studies reporting stimulation parameters and outcomes (n47 studies, 52 experiments). In initial exploratory analyses with univariate tests, we find that parameters, such as the intensity and continuity of stimulation (duty cycle, DC) show statistical trends towards likely TUS neural enhancement or suppression of function. Machine-learning analyses were limited by the currently small sample size. Given that human TUS sample sizes are expected to increase, predictability on the directionality of TUS effects could improve if a database is available. Therefore, we establish an database and resource for the systematic reporting of TUS parameters and outcomes to assist in greater precision in TUS use for brain stimulation and neuromodulation. The paper concludes with a selective review of human clinical TUS studies illustrating how hypotheses on the directionality of TUS effects could be developed for empirical testing in the intended clinical application, not limited to the examples provided.

item.title: Loose coupling between Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels and release sensors as a synaptic correlate of higher-order brain function
item.author: Simone Brachtendorf
item.content:encoded: In the mature neocortex, functionally distinct areas are built by the same archetypes of neurons, but depending on the area, these neurons and their synapses are engaged in very different functions, ranging from lower-order processing of sensory information to higher-order associations and cognitive functions. We found significant differences in the functional presynaptic nanoarchitectures of the same types of pyramidal neuron synapses, depending on whether they are located in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) or in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) of mice. Mature synapses in PFC operated with loose microdomain coupling, as opposed to tight nanodomain coupling in S1. These differences were associated with significant differences in synaptic timing, efficacy, and plasticity between areas. Our data suggest that the mature neocortex uses tuning of synaptic topographies to specialize seemingly identical types of neurons for their required function. They suggest that microdomain coupling in pyramidal neuron synapses could be a presynaptic structure-function correlate of higher-order neocortical functions.

item.title: Organization of neuropeptide signaling: cross-species insights from small model organisms
item.author: Meet Zandawala, Alessandro Filosa, Isabel Beets
item.content:encoded: Neuropeptides are ancient signaling molecules that modulate neural circuit function and behavior across the animal kingdom. Model organisms such as Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and zebrafish serve as powerful in vivo models for deciphering the organization of neuropeptidergic signaling, owing to their smaller nervous systems, genetic tractability, and the growing availability of neural connectomes. In this article, we review how these organisms have advanced current understanding of neuropeptidergic transmission across three interconnected themes: (i) the roles of peptides in sensory–motor transformations, (ii) the conservation and divergence of peptidergic expression and network architecture across species, and (iii) the diversity of neurotransmission strategies employed by single neurons. Finally, we highlight recent technological innovations as well as open questions that could shape this field in the coming years.

item.title: foxQ2 marks fast-acting interneurons including dopaminergic neurons of mushroom bodies and central complex in the beetle Tribolium castaneum
item.author: Ying Pang
item.content:encoded: The brain is one of the most complex animal organs, and the development of the many different neuron types remains enigmatic. A set of brain-specific transcription factors is involved in brain patterning, but their specific contributions mostly remain to be elucidated, including . This transcription factor is conserved in anterior neuroectodermal patterning of most animals, while it has been lost from vertebrates. The contribution of -positive neurons to the adult brain has remained enigmatic. Here, we use our enhancer trap, immunostainings, and our newly established beetle system to categorize -positive neurons into nine clusters with different projection patterns. All clusters contain neurons with the fast-activating neurotransmitters acetylcholine and glutamate, while no -positive neuron is GABA-ergic or serotonin-positive. Interestingly, we found that many dopaminergic neurons were positive and homologize them with dopaminergic neurons of the PPL2c, PPM1, and PPL1 cluster described in the brain. Our results show that marks subsets of fast-acting interneurons contributing to the higher-order brain centers and . Taken together, our work expands the known functional range of genes from sensory and neurosecretory cell specification to interneurons involved in the function of higher-order brain centers.

item.title: Heterogeneous responses to embryonic critical period perturbations within the Drosophila larval locomotor circuit
item.author: Richard A Baines
item.content:encoded: As developing neural circuits become functional, they undergo a phase of heightened plasticity that facilitates network tuning in response to intrinsic and/or extrinsic stimuli. These developmental windows are termed critical periods (CPs) because perturbations during but not outside the CP can lead to lasting changes, such as the formation of sub-optimal or unstable networks. How separate but connected elements within a network might respond differently to a CP perturbation is not well understood. To study this, we used the locomotor network of the larva as a model and heat stress as a CP stimulus that has ecological relevance. When embryos experienced heat stress, the subsequent development of their locomotor network was changed, creating larvae with reduced crawling speed and decreased network stability. Developing body wall muscles and central neurons are sensitive to heat stress perturbations during distinct, consecutive phases of embryogenesis. Within the CNS, transient embryonic CP perturbation leads to increased synaptic drive from premotor interneurons to motoneurons, which in turn adopt reduced excitability. In contrast, the peripheral neuromuscular junction maintains normal synaptic transmission, despite significant structural changes. Thus, connected elements respond differentially to a CP perturbation, suggesting a sequence, or hierarchy of network adjustment during the CP.

item.title: Open source laser-scanning photostimulation for neuroscience with Zapit
item.author: Thomas D Mrsic-Flogel
item.content:encoded: Optogenetic tools are indispensable for understanding the causal neural mechanisms underlying animal behavior, providing millisecond-precision control over genetically defined neural populations. Random-access laser-scanning optogenetics is a powerful and underutilized method for transiently manipulating cortical activity in mice. Despite the utility of this technique, no general-purpose open-source implementation currently exists, and potential users need expertise across optics, real-time hardware control, and programming. This represents a major barrier to adoption, particularly for newly established research groups. Here we present ‘Zapit’, the first open-source general-purpose platform for random-access laser-scanning optogenetic experiments in head-fixed mice. Zapit is fully documented, has a user-friendly GUI, works in stereotaxic coordinates, and comes with easy-to-build hardware options that extend functionality beyond any published system. We validate Zapit’s performance through electrophysiological recordings and cortical photoinhibition in behaving mice. Zapit is a novel and innovative tool with the potential to democratize laser-scanning optogenetics and significantly increase uptake throughout the scientific community.

item.title: Evidence supports constituency-based syntax, movement, and unpronounced elements
item.author: Hiroki Fujita
item.content:encoded: Gibson advocates dependency grammar [1], contrasting it with constituency-based accounts that posit movement and phonologically null (unpronounced) syntactic elements [2,3]. Dependency grammar represents sentence structure through word-to-word relations, whereas constituency-based accounts represent sentence structure by grouping words into larger hierarchical constituents. Movement accounts for cases in which a constituent appears in one position but is interpreted in another. For example, in ‘Who did you call?’, ‘Who’ appears sentence-initially but is interpreted as the object of ‘call’; this is analysed as movement from the object position to the sentence-initial position.

item.title: Dependency grammar remains the simplest theory of grammar: a reply to Fujita
item.author: Edward Gibson
item.content:encoded: In the original article [1], I claimed that dependency grammar is the simplest theory of grammar. All theories of grammar have rules for connecting words together to make larger units. In dependency grammar, these connections are directly between words. In phrase structure grammars, there is slightly more structure than in dependency grammar, consisting of nonterminal categories for the connected elements, such as the noun phrase and the verb phrase. I argued that these two alternatives are somewhat interchangeable.

Modulation of human dorsal root ganglion neuron excitability by Nav1.7 inhibition
item.author: Tomás Osorno
item.content:encoded: Nav1.7 voltage-gated sodium channels are strongly expressed in human primary pain-sensing neurons (nociceptors), and selective Nav1.7 inhibitors have been developed as possible therapeutic agents for treating pain, so far with disappointing clinical results. In contrast, a selective Nav1.8 channel inhibitor (suzetrigine) has had successful clinical trials. Because nociceptors express both Nav1.7 and Nav1.8 channels, it is of interest to compare effects of Nav1.7 and Nav1.8 inhibitors on the excitability of human nociceptors. To compare with previous results with suzetrigine, we characterized the effects of a selective Nav1.7 inhibitor, AM-2099, on action potential generation and repetitive firing of dissociated human dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, studied at 37°C. Inhibition of Nav1.7 channels by 600 nM AM-2099 generally produced a substantial depolarizing shift of action potential threshold, an increase in rheobase, a decrease in action potential upstroke velocity, decrease in action potential peak, and prolongation of the refractory period. Compared to inhibition of Nav1.8 channels, inhibition of Nav1.7 channels had larger effects on threshold and maximal upstroke velocity, while action potential peak was reduced similarly by both. Nav1.8 inhibition produced much more dramatic reduction of repetitive firing than Nav1.7 inhibition. The results show that although the excitability of human DRG neurons is affected by inhibition of Nav1.7 channels, most notably by an increase in threshold and increase in refractory period, repetitive firing of the neurons in response to strong stimuli is little affected.

item.title: Large language models poorly capture how word order shapes representations of sentence meaning in the human brain
item.author: Shinsuke Suzuki
item.content:encoded: Large language models based on the transformer architecture are now capable of producing human-like language. But do they encode and process linguistic meaning in a human-like way? Here, we address this question by analysing 7T fMRI data from 30 participants reading 108 sentences each. These sentences are carefully designed to disentangle sentence structure from word meaning, thereby testing whether transformer representations of sentence meaning resemble those formed by the brain. Using representational similarity analysis, we compared representations from eight transformers and eleven other semantic models to brain activity in language regions of interest. We found that while transformer models match brain representations better than models that completely ignore word order, all transformers poorly match human brain representations of sentences that require sensitivity to structural relations such as semantic roles (who did what to whom). Further, transformers were significantly inferior to models explicitly designed to encode the structural relations between words. Our results provide insight into the nature of sentence representation in the brain, highlighting the critical role of sentence structure. They also cast doubt on the claim that transformers represent sentence meaning similarly to the human brain.

item.title: Mapping the topographic organization of the human zona incerta using diffusion MRI
item.author: Violet Liu
item.content:encoded: The zona incerta (ZI) is a deep brain region originally described by Auguste Forel as an ‘immensely confusing area about which nothing can be said’. Despite the elusive nature of this structure, mounting evidence supports the role of the ZI and surrounding regions across a diverse range of brain functions and as a candidate target for neuromodulatory therapies. Using in vivo diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and data-driven connectivity, we identify a topographic organization between the ZI and neocortex. Specifically, our methods identify a rostral–caudal gradient predominantly connecting the frontopolar and ventral prefrontal cortices with the rostral ZI, and the primary sensorimotor cortices with the caudal ZI. Moreover, we demonstrate how clustering and gradient approaches build complementary evidence including facilitating the mapping of a central region of the ZI, connected with the dorsal prefrontal cortex. These results were shown to be replicable across multiple datasets and at the individual subject level, building evidence for the important role of the ZI in mediating frontal lobe-associated tasks, ranging from motor to cognitive to emotional control. Finally, we consider the impact of this topographic organization on the refinement of neuromodulatory targets. These results pave the way for an increasingly detailed understanding of ZI substructures, and considerations for in vivo targeting of the ZI for neuromodulation.

item.title: Morphology and ultrastructure of pharyngeal sense organs of Drosophila larvae
item.author: Vincent Richter
item.content:encoded: This study provides a comprehensive ultrastructural analysis of the pharyngeal sensory system in larvae, focusing on the four major pharyngeal sense organs: the ventral pharyngeal sensilla (VPS), dorsal pharyngeal sensilla (DPS), dorsal pharyngeal organ (DPO), and posterior pharyngeal sensilla (PPS). Our analysis revealed 15 sensilla across these organs, comprising four mechanosensory, nine chemosensory, and two dual-function sensilla. We identified 35 Type I neurons (6 mechanosensory and 29 chemosensory) and 6 Type II neurons with putative chemosensory functions. Additional sensory structures, including papilla sensilla and chordotonal organs in the cephalopharyngeal region, were characterized. This detailed mapping and classification of pharyngeal sensory structures completes their structural characterization and provides a foundation for future anatomical and functional studies of sensory perception in insects. This work represents a significant step toward a complete analysis of the larval sensory system, providing new opportunities for investigating how an organism processes sensory information to navigate and interact with its environment.

item.title: Selection-for-prediction: rethinking early cognitive development
item.author: Stella F. Lourenco
item.content:encoded: For decades, core knowledge accounts have proposed that early cognition is organized by innate, domain-specific conceptual or concept-like representations of objects, physical events, number, and agents. I propose a different starting point: infants’ behaviors may arise from domain-general attentional priors—evolutionarily shaped selection biases—interacting with perceptual mechanisms that organize information and support perceptual prediction, rather than from abstract, postperceptual representations. Attentional priors favor ecologically consequential information, including continuity, contact, and synchrony. When such information is disrupted, perceptual prediction error—rather than conceptual contradiction—may produce violation-of-expectation effects. Grounded in constraints on visual input and neural processing, this framework accounts for early successes and systematic failures, suggesting that development begins with perceptual-attentional mechanisms that shape selection, organization, prediction, and learning.

item.title: From sample diversity to interpretive convergence
item.author: Taro Murakami
item.content:encoded: Generative artificial intelligence tools are being increasingly used by scientists, especially as writing aids for researchers outside English-dominant institutions. However, these tools might narrow interpretations even when applied to increasingly diverse samples. Sampling diversity will not be enough to broaden behavioural science if interpretive diversity is lost.

item.title: Olfactory combinatorial coding supports risk–reward decision-making in Caenorhabditis elegans
item.author: William G Ryan
item.content:encoded: Olfactory-driven behaviors are essential for animal survival, but mechanisms for decoding olfactory inputs remain poorly understood. We have used whole-network Ca imaging to study olfactory coding in . We show that the odorant 1-octanol is encoded combinatorially in the periphery as both an attractant and a repellent. These inputs are integrated centrally, and their relative strengths determine the sensitivity and valence of the behavioral response through modulation of locomotory reversals and speed. The balance of these pathways also dictates the activity of the locomotory command interneurons, which control locomotory reversals. This balance serves as a regulatory node for response modulation, allowing to weigh opportunities and hazards in its environment when formulating behavioral responses. Thus, an odorant can be encoded simultaneously as inputs of opposite valence, focusing attention on the integration of these inputs in determining perception, response, and plasticity.

item.title: Motor unit mechanisms of speed control in mouse locomotion
item.author: Samuel J Sober
item.content:encoded: During locomotion, the coordinated activity of dozens of muscles shapes the kinematic features of each stride, including systematic changes in limb movement across walking speed. Motor units, each of which consists of a single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates, contribute to the total activation of each muscle through their recruitment and firing rate when active. However, it remains unknown how the nervous system controls locomotor speed by changing the firing of individual motor units. To address this, we combined quantitative behavioral analysis of mouse locomotion with single motor unit recordings from the lateral and long heads of the triceps brachii, which drive monoarticular extension of the elbow and biarticular movements of the elbow and shoulder, respectively. In contrast to prior studies employing bulk electromyography (EMG) to examine muscle activity, our recordings revealed the diversity of spike patterning across motor units, as well as systematic differences in motor unit activity across muscles and locomotor speeds. First, motor unit activity differed significantly across the lateral and long heads, suggesting differential control of these two closely apposed elbow extensor muscles. Second, we found that individual units were recruited probabilistically (during only a subset of strides), showing that the highly repeatable bulk EMG signals observed across strides, in fact, reflect varying subsets of individual motor units. Finally, although recruitment probability and firing rate both increased at faster walking speeds, increases in recruitment were proportionally larger than rate changes, and recruitment of individual units accompanied changes in limb kinematics. Together, these results reveal how the firing of individual motor units varies systematically across muscles and walking speeds to produce flexible locomotor behavior.

item.title: Strong mnemonic prediction errors increase cognitive control, attention, and arousal
item.author: Jenna Jokhani
item.content:encoded: Ongoing experience is continuously processed in the context of past events. Divergence between current experience and memory-based predictions (i.e., a mnemonic prediction error; MPE) is theorized to be a signal that encoding, as opposed to retrieval, should be prioritized. We asked how MPEs place demands on control and attention-related processes, and whether these demands differ as a function of prediction strength. We investigated these questions across two experiments, wherein we recorded scalp electroencephalography and/or pupillometry as 101 young human adults performed an associative memory task. Strong MPEs, more so than weak MPEs, increased physiological indices of cognitive control (frontal theta), attention (posterior alpha and pupil size), and arousal (pupil size). Greater cognitive control (frontal theta) during strong MPEs promoted better learning of prediction-violating (i.e., unexpected) stimuli. Collectively, these findings reveal multiple pathways through which the mind and brain respond adaptively to violations of strong mnemonic predictions.

item.title: Complementary stable and dynamic prelimbic ensembles encode learned threat value underlying generalization and discrimination
item.author: Pedro M Ogallar
item.content:encoded: Adaptive behavior requires assigning emotional value to sensory cues and generalizing to similar stimuli. The prelimbic cortex (PL) is critical for threat expression and discrimination, yet its neuronal ensembles undergo substantial turnover over time. How stable population codes emerge despite this reorganization remains unknown. Using longitudinal calcium imaging in freely moving mice, we tracked PL activity for 30 days during auditory discriminative fear learning and retrieval. Despite substantial ensemble turnover, stable graded representations persisted in PL populations. A generalized linear model showed that the tone threat value explained graded activity better than freezing, indicating that PL primarily encodes stimulus significance. Population similarity across stimulus presentations was highest for shock-associated and highly generalized tones, suggesting a stable population code underlying threat generalization. Stable neurons preserved graded gradients across sessions, whereas learning modulated the rate of dynamic frequency-selective neurons. Together, these populations enabled stable threat-value coding despite ongoing ensemble reorganization.

item.title: A mechanistic theory of planning in prefrontal cortex
item.author: Timothy E Behrens
item.content:encoded: Planning is critical for adaptive behaviour in a changing world, because it lets us anticipate the future and adjust our actions accordingly. While prefrontal cortex is crucial for this process, it remains unknown how planning is implemented in neural circuits. Prefrontal representations were recently discovered in simpler sequence memory tasks, where different populations of neurons represent different future time points. We demonstrate that combining such representations with the ubiquitous principle of neural attractor dynamics allows circuits to solve much richer problems, including planning. This is achieved by embedding the environment structure directly in synaptic connections to implement an attractor network that infers desirable futures. The resulting ‘spacetime attractor’ excels at planning in challenging tasks known to depend on the prefrontal cortex. Recurrent neural networks trained by gradient descent on such tasks learn a solution that precisely recapitulates the spacetime attractor – in representation, in dynamics, and in connectivity. Analyses of networks trained across different environment structures reveal a generalisation mechanism that rapidly reconfigures the world model used for planning, without the need for synaptic plasticity. The spacetime attractor is a testable mechanistic theory of planning. If true, it would provide a path towards detailed mechanistic understanding of how prefrontal cortex structures adaptive behaviour.

item.title: Tumor innervation in non-central nervous system tumors: origins, mechanisms, and phenotypic plasticity
item.author: Yonghui Zhang, Zhixin Ye, Ying Wang, Siying Tang, Gang Chen
item.content:encoded: The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of solid tumor biology. We synthesize recent advances in cancer neuroscience, focusing on three interconnected themes: the cellular origins of tumor-associated nerves, the molecular mechanisms that govern neural recruitment and remodeling, and the resulting phenotypic plasticity within the tumor microenvironment. Tumor innervation arises through axon extension from pre-existing nerves, recruitment of neural precursors, and neuron-like transdifferentiation of non-neuronal cells. These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. The functional consequences of innervation are context-dependent, with sympathetic, parasympathetic, and sensory inputs exerting distinct effects across tumor types and stages. We conclude by outlining key challenges and future directions for therapeutic translation.

item.title: An integrated human forebrain organoid reveals microglia-mediated CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell recruitment and neuroimmune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease pathology
item.author: Zitian Wang
item.content:encoded: Genetic evidence implicates immune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet the neuroimmune mechanisms operating in human tissue remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a modular human forebrain organoid platform that systematically integrates human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia and CD8 T cells to reconstitute multicellular AD pathology. This system enables functional interrogation of both innate and adaptive immune components in a human-relevant context. Using this platform, we demonstrate that microglia mediate amyloid-β clearance and neuronal maturation but also drive inflammatory activation and recruit CD8 T cells through CCL4/5 signaling via CCR1/5 and CXCR3, establishing a neuroinflammatory feedback loop. Pharmacological targeting of CCR5 or CXCR3 blocks T cell recruitment and modulates autophagy in a microglia-dependent manner. This modular organoid platform provides a versatile tool for dissecting neuron–immune interactions and enables cell-type-specific therapeutic screening in human neuroinflammatory disease models.

item.title: Multiplexed CRISPRi reveals a transcriptional switch between KLF activators and repressors in the maturing neocortex
item.author: Sacha B Nelson
item.content:encoded: A critical phase of mammalian brain development takes place after birth. Neurons of the mouse neocortex undergo dramatic changes in their morphology, physiology, and synaptic connections during the first postnatal month, while properties of immature neurons, such as the capacity for robust axon outgrowth, are lost. The genetic and epigenetic programs controlling prenatal development are well studied, but our understanding of the transcriptional mechanisms that regulate postnatal neuronal maturation is comparatively lacking. By integrating chromatin accessibility and gene expression data from two subtypes of neocortical pyramidal neurons in the neonatal and maturing brain, we predicted a role for the Krüppel-like factor (KLF) family of transcription factors in the developmental regulation of neonatally expressed genes. Using a multiplexed CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) knockdown strategy, we found that a shift in expression from KLF activators (Klf6, Klf7) to repressors (Klf9, Klf13) during early postnatal development functions as a transcriptional ‘switch’ to first activate, then repress a set of shared targets with cytoskeletal functions including and . We demonstrate that this switch is buffered by redundancy between KLF paralogs, which our multiplexed CRISPRi strategy is equipped to overcome and study. Our results indicate that competition between activators and repressors within the KLF family regulates a conserved component of the postnatal maturation program that may underlie the loss of intrinsic axon growth in maturing neurons. This could facilitate the transition from axon growth to synaptic refinement required to stabilize mature circuits.

Apolipoprotein E4 and immune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease: mechanisms and therapeutic implications
item.author: Hao Shi, Yang Zhao, Wei Zhu, Yan-Jiang Wang, Xian-Le Bu
item.content:encoded: Emerging evidence suggests that apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) functions as an organizer of brain–periphery immune crosstalk, coupling maladaptive microglial states with peripheral immune remodeling to establish a self-reinforcing neuroimmune loop that may accelerate the progression of Alzheimer’s disease. In the central nervous system, APOE4 pushes microglia away from homeostatic surveillance toward metabolically stressed, inflammatory, and synaptotoxic phenotypes, thereby weakening pathological protein clearance and promoting neurodegeneration. In the periphery, APOE4 primes innate and adaptive immune cells toward a pro-inflammatory state, creating a reservoir that can communicate with the diseased brain and infiltrate it. In addition, APOE4 erodes the separation between central and peripheral immune compartments, enabling bidirectional immune crosstalk that amplifies neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. In this review, we synthesize evidence for APOE4-driven central and peripheral immune dysregulation; discuss therapeutic opportunities for targeting the APOE4 immune axis; and highlight the need for human-derived, longitudinal, cross-tissue studies to identify causal, stage-specific, and targetable immune nodes for precision intervention.

Today Henri Matisse’s the red studio is considered one of the landmarks of modern art, seen by thousands of visitors at the Museum of Modern art in New York. But before arriving there in 1948 it spent more than a decade hanging in a London nightclub.
When Matisse painted the red studio in 1911 it was one of the strangest pictures anyone had ever seen - a room almost completely consumed by red – furniture reduced to outlines, paintings hanging on walls that barely seem to exist, and a grandfather clock with 12 numbers but no hands. Even Matisse wasn't entirely sure what he had created and nobody wanted to buy it.
So how did a painting that even its creator struggle to understand, go from rejection and obscurity to becoming a masterpiece of modern art and what was it doing in a London nightclub in the first place?

item.title: In vivo virus-free lineage tracing and live imaging reveal that NeuroD1 does not reprogram microglia into neurons
item.author: Yuxin Li
item.content:encoded: In situ glia-to-neuron conversion induced by a single transcription factor is a promising regenerative strategy for treating central nervous system injuries and neurodegenerative diseases. Previous studies reported that NeuroD1 can induce microglia-to-neuron cross-lineage conversion and improve recovery after brain injury. However, these findings remain controversial. To examine the ability of NeuroD1 in inducing microglia-to-neuron conversion, we employed virus-free genetic lineage tracing systems in mice to specifically induce NeuroD1 expression in microglia and track the cell fate of NeuroD1-expressing cells at multiple timepoints. Meanwhile, we longitudinally monitored NeuroD1-expressing microglia via two-photon imaging and characterized their transcriptional profile by single-cell RNA sequencing. All observations across these methods revealed that NeuroD1-expressing cells retained their microglia identity and cannot convert into neurons, under either physiological and injury conditions. Instead, sustained expression of NeuroD1 induced microglial apoptosis in vivo. Collectively, our findings provide strong evidence that NeuroD1 is not sufficient to induce microglia-to-neuron conversion. This study further highlights the importance of rigorous lineage tracing and cell fate mapping strategies for validating in situ glia-to-neuron conversion.

item.title: Individual dopaminergic neurons induce unique, yet overlapping combinations of behavioural modulations, including safety learning, memory retrieval, and acute locomotion
item.author: Oliver Kobler
item.content:encoded: Two evolutionary highly conserved functions of dopamine are to carry ‘teaching’ signals during associative learning and to control movement. In mammals and humans, these functions are generally thought to be produced by different populations of neurons. Here, we investigated in the larva of whether both these functions can be induced by the same individual dopaminergic neurons in the central brain. Focusing on the dopaminergic neurons of the DL1 cluster, we asked whether the optogenetic activation of individual neurons established associative punishment and/or safety memories, controlled the retrieval of the established memories, and acutely modulated locomotion. We found that each neuron had a unique yet overlapping set of behavioural effects. Several individual neurons both established a memory and modulated acute locomotion by increasing the animals’ bending and decreasing their velocity. Our results demonstrate that individual dopaminergic neurons can fulfil a surprisingly broad range of functions in different behavioural contexts. Given the highly conserved roles of the dopaminergic system across the animal kingdom, this study raises the question whether a similarly diverse functionality can be found also in other animals, including humans.

Age is a primary risk factor for many of these disorders, yet systematic analysis of how the dopamine system changes during healthy aging remains relatively understudied. In this review, we first examine the impact of healthy aging on the dopamine system across sexes and species, including flies, mice, rats, and humans. We next consider the neuroadaptive mechanisms that sustain dopamine neuron function with age. Finally, we contrast the molecular mechanisms of age-related neurodegenerative diseases with those of healthy aging, exploring the possibility that loss of neuroadaptive reserve drives dopamine neurodegeneration. Elucidating these neuroadaptive mechanisms could offer a path toward preserving dopamine neuron function across the lifespan and potentially preventing age-related neurodegeneration.

item.title: Sound asleep, yet still listening: auditory processing during human sleep

item.content:encoded: Sleepers can wake to their name, but ignore louder irrelevant sounds, a paradox that suggests more than simple sensory gating. Growing evidence reveals flexible auditory coupling during human sleep, ranging from complete disconnection to high-level cognitive processing and even to physical responses. Here, we synthesize the multiple cognitive levels at which auditory stimuli are processed (or not) during human sleep and outline factors modulating this processing. Moments of sensory isolation may promote restoration and memory consolidation, while moments of environmental coupling enable threat detection. We speculate that no single optimal balance exists; rather, the ideal degree of sensory coupling shifts with individuals and contexts. Chronic dysregulation of this balance may contribute to the clinical picture of sleep disorders, including insomnia and hypersomnia.

item.title: Sleep-dependent microglial functions in Alzheimer’s disease
item.author: Sara Calafate, Renzo Mancuso
item.content:encoded: Sleep is a fundamental regulator of brain homeostasis, yet how distinct brain cell types contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, actively regulate neuroinflammatory tone, metabolic waste clearance, and synaptic remodeling, thereby contributing to neural circuit maintenance and proteostasis. Delineating the different functions played by microglia during specific brain states, such as sleep, represents an active area of research. In this article, we review a growing literature supporting the notion that sleep dynamically shapes microglial functional outputs. We further suggest that the failure of the sleep–microglia axis may represent an important component of the molecular framework of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), contributing to disease progression. Finally, we discuss preclinical and clinical evidence suggesting that sleep-targeting interventions may modulate AD pathology, and highlight the possibility that restoring sleep physiology could recalibrate microglial homeostatic functions and slow disease progression.

GABAB receptor signalling in pre- and postsynaptic domains of neurons is often overlooked, despite the strong inhibition it produces. Importantly, GABAB receptors are diversely phosphorylated and interact with various auxiliary subunits to modify function. item.author: Fiorella Del Popolo Cristaldi, Leah Banellis, Gioia Bottesi, Micah G. Allen
item.content:encoded: For decades, accuracy in detecting internal bodily signals has been considered an important component of emotional experience. Yet this link remains elusive. Across methods and domains, interoceptive accuracy shows inconsistent associations with emotion and psychopathology. We argue this mismatch reflects a hierarchy of interoceptive processing: accuracy measures capture how bodily signals are detected, whereas emotion depends on metacognitive appraisals of what those signals mean, their reliability, and what they imply about the self. We introduce interoceptive self-appraisal (ISA) as a higher-order process through which bodily sensations are interpreted in context and assigned significance. ISA provides a framework for investigating affective vulnerability and developmental pathways to psychopathology. By integrating disparate theories of bodily appraisal, we outline a roadmap for interoception research.

item.content:encoded: In a recent study, Routh and colleagues demonstrated that the circadian clock regulates microglia-directed synaptic refinement during a critical period of neurodevelopment in mice, in a sex-dependent manner. item.title: Time after time: neural codes of speech comprehension
item.author: Laura Gwilliams
item.content:encoded: The acoustic signal of speech is fleeting and unfolds linearly; yet listeners must derive temporally extended and hierarchically organized linguistic structures to comprehend it. This article reviews evidence that the human brain transforms the transient auditory signal into neural representations that are persistent, parallel, and time-stamped. First, neural persistence allows information to remain available after it has disappeared from the acoustic input. Second, parallel encoding of recent inputs across multiple levels of language structure enables composition and interactions across the speech hierarchy. Third, dynamic neural representations encode both content and elapsed time, providing a flexible mechanism for preserving sequence order. Together, these representational properties reveal how the human brain transforms a continuously disappearing signal into temporally extended linguistic structures.
